genZNote: Punches actual holes in a hair shaft in the lab test named for exactly that — and doesn't light up under a Wood's lamp like its cousin does.

morphology.shape: Septate hyphae with spiral (corkscrew) hyphae and grape-like clusters of microconidia
morphology.size: Microconidia ~2-4 µm; smooth thin-walled cigar-shaped macroconidia less numerous

habitat.naturalHabitat: Skin and fur of rodents and other animals (zoophilic strains); soil (geophilic strains); human skin (anthropophilic strains)
habitat.hostAssociation: Zoonotic and anthropophilic strains both exist — transmission from rodents/animals or person-to-person
habitat.reservoir: Rodents, other animals, soil, and infected humans depending on strain

microscopy.stain: KOH wet mount of skin scrapings; lactophenol cotton blue of culture
microscopy.appearance: Septate hyphae; distinctive spiral (corkscrew) hyphae and grape-like clusters of round microconidia on culture

culture.media: Sabouraud dextrose agar, dermatophyte test medium (DTM)
culture.growthCharacteristics: Obligate aerobe; grows over 1-2 weeks; turns DTM red
culture.colonyMorphology: White to cream, powdery to cottony surface
culture.pigmentation: Variable, tan to yellow-brown reverse pigment

identificationClues: Spiral (corkscrew) hyphae and grape-like clusters of microconidia on culture — a distinctive morphologic clue
Hair perforation test positive (wedge-shaped perforations), unlike T. rubrum which is typically negative
Does not fluoresce under a Wood's lamp, distinguishing it from Microsporum canis
Common cause of tinea pedis, tinea corporis, and inflammatory tinea capitis

diseases: Inflammatory tinea capitis, particularly with zoophilic strains
virulenceFactors: Keratinase enzymes enabling invasion of skin, hair, and nail keratin
Can invade the hair shaft in either ectothrix or endothrix patterns depending on strain
clinicalImportance.transmission: Direct contact with infected animals (zoophilic strains, e.g., rodents), soil (geophilic strains), or person-to-person/fomite contact (anthropophilic strains, e.g., shared shower floors, locker rooms)
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: One of the most common dermatophytes causing tinea pedis and tinea corporis worldwide; zoophilic strains tend to cause a more inflammatory reaction than anthropophilic dermatophytes
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: The hair perforation test and lack of Wood's lamp fluorescence help distinguish T. mentagrophytes from T. rubrum and M. canis respectively when culture morphology is ambiguous

examFacts.shape: Septate hyphae, spiral hyphae, grape-like microconidia clusters
examFacts.importantDisease: Tinea pedis, tinea corporis, inflammatory tinea capitis
examFacts.importantTest: In vitro hair perforation test (positive); Wood's lamp (negative, unlike M. canis)
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Hair-perforation-test-positive dermatophyte with spiral hyphae — does not fluoresce under Wood's lamp, unlike Microsporum canis
